intro:
These exercises move from reading a trait definition to publishing one as a deliberate API choice. The chapter's mental model is a triangle: the trait names a method set, each concrete type carries its own impl block, and call sites name the trait either as a generic bound or as a dyn object. The exercises drill the three decisions that follow from that model: where dispatch is resolved (compile time versus a vtable), whether to commit an output with an associated type, and whether the trait must remain object-safe so it can live behind dyn Trait, whether that is Box<dyn Trait> or &dyn Trait.

The set builds toward a single production judgment. You read the static-dispatch RetryPolicy example to see how an associated type and a where-clause pin an output to bool, extend it with a second policy, then move to the dyn plugin pipeline to see why object safety is what lets unrelated types share one boxed list. The debugging and design exercises close the loop: a generic method silently forecloses dyn, and deciding object safety up front is cheap while retrofitting it later is a breaking change.

exerciseSolutions.title: Separate the trait, the impl, and the call site
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The three corners of the triangle are the trait, the concrete type, and the call site. The trait is a named set of methods with no data of its own (here RetryPolicy with decide, label, and should_log). The concrete type is the data (FixedLimit { max: u32 }). The call site is the code that names the trait, either as a bound on a generic parameter (fn evaluate

(... ) where P: RetryPolicy) or as a dyn object. The impl block is the third, separate thing that links a type to a trait: impl RetryPolicy for FixedLimit. It is neither part of the struct definition nor part of the trait definition. Because the link lives in an independent impl block, the same struct can implement Display, Iterator, and RetryPolicy without any of them referencing the others. Each impl is written separately and only the type name ties them together; Display never mentions RetryPolicy, and RetryPolicy never mentions Display. Capability is added in layers, so a type accumulates unrelated behaviors without a class hierarchy declaring them all in one place. That is the concrete meaning of composition over inheritance in this model: you assemble capabilities by adding impls rather than inheriting a fixed bundle from a base class. The dispatch decision is made at the call site, not at the trait or the impl. The trait only declares the method set and the impl only supplies bodies; neither commits to how the method is reached. The call site chooses: a generic bound monomorphizes into a direct call resolved at compile time, while a dyn object routes the call through a vtable at runtime. The same trait and the same impl serve both, because the choice of dispatch is the caller's.
criteria: Identifies the trait as the named method set, the concrete type (FixedLimit's data) as the data, and the call site as where the trait is named as a bound or dyn object.
States the impl block is the separate thing linking type to trait, distinct from the type definition.
Explains capability is added in independent impl layers, so one struct carries many unrelated impls that do not reference each other.
Locates the dispatch choice at the call site (generic bound versus dyn), not at the trait or impl.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the RetryPolicy associated type and where-clause
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Self::Decision resolves to bool for FixedLimit. That is declared in the impl block by the line type Decision = bool;. The trait leaves Decision abstract (type Decision; with no body), and each implementer must pick a concrete output; FixedLimit commits to bool. So inside decide, the return type Self::Decision is literally bool, and the body attempts < self.max produces a bool directly.

The where-clause P: RetryPolicy<Decision = bool> on evaluate lets the function assume decide returns exactly bool, not just some opaque Self::Decision. Without that bound, the compiler would only know decide returns an unspecified associated type, which format! could not necessarily display and which the caller could not reason about. With the bound, evaluate can write format!("{} => {}", policy.label(), policy.decide(attempts)) and rely on the bool implementing Display, with no turbofish, no trait import for the output, and no conversion. The associated type plus the equality constraint pin the output so the call site can trust it.

evaluate calls label and decide. FixedLimit overrides label (it returns "fixed-limit" instead of the trait's default "policy"). It does not override should_log, so the default method body return true is inherited unchanged. For FixedLimit { max: 3 } and evaluate(&policy, 2), decide(2) evaluates 2 < 3, which is true, and label returns "fixed-limit", so the first println! prints fixed-limit => true. The second line prints policy.should_log(), which uses the inherited default returning true, so it prints log = true.

Decision is an associated type rather than a trait-level generic parameter because each policy has exactly one natural output: FixedLimit decides with a bool and never with anything else. An associated type encodes that one-output-per-implementer fact, so the implementer commits once (type Decision = bool;) and call sites write Self::Decision with nothing to disambiguate. If type Decision were instead a trait-level generic, written RetryPolicy<D>, the same type could in principle implement the trait for several D, so the compiler could no longer infer which instantiation a call site means. Callers would then have to spell out the parameter, for example with turbofish (evaluate::<FixedLimit, bool>) or extra type annotations, and the bound RetryPolicy<Decision = bool> that reads so cleanly today would become a positional RetryPolicy<bool>. The associated type keeps the single answer implicit and the call sites free of that ceremony.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Predicted output and the reasoning behind each line.
criteria: States Self::Decision is bool because the impl declares type Decision = bool.
Explains the where-clause guarantees decide returns bool, so format! displays it directly with no turbofish or conversion.
Notes label is overridden by FixedLimit while should_log is inherited from the default method.
Predicts the output lines fixed-limit => true and log = true.

Explains Decision is an associated type because each policy has one natural output, and that a trait-level generic <D> would force callers to disambiguate the instantiation with turbofish or extra annotations.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a second RetryPolicy with a default override
exerciseSolutions.solution:
AlwaysRetry implements RetryPolicy with type Decision = bool, which is what lets it be passed to evaluate unchanged: evaluate's bound is RetryPolicy<Decision = bool>, so any implementer that commits its associated type to bool satisfies the signature without any modification to evaluate. The dispatch is still static, monomorphized per concrete type, so adding a new policy costs nothing at the call site.

decide ignores its attempts argument and returns true, expressed by naming the parameter _attempts (or prefixing with an underscore) to signal it is intentionally unused. label is overridden to return "always", replacing the trait default "policy". should_log is overridden to return false, replacing the default that returned true. Overriding a default method simply means writing the method body in the impl block; if you omit it, the trait's default stands, which is exactly why FixedLimit could inherit should_log in the previous exercise.

With these in place, evaluate(&AlwaysRetry, 99) computes label() then decide(99). label returns "always" and decide returns true regardless of the 99, so the formatted string is "always => true". AlwaysRetry.should_log() returns the overridden false. Both results reuse the existing evaluate function and the existing RetryPolicy trait without changing either; the only new code is the struct and its impl block.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: AlwaysRetry satisfies the Decision = bool bound and overrides two defaults; evaluate is reused unchanged.
criteria: Sets type Decision = bool and compiles against fn evaluate without modifying evaluate.
decide returns true for any attempts value, ignoring the argument via _attempts.
label returns "always" and should_log returns false, both overriding the trait defaults.
evaluate(&AlwaysRetry, 99) yields always => true and AlwaysRetry.should_log() yields false (AlwaysRetry is a unit struct, so it is spelled without braces).

exerciseSolutions.title: Make a Plugin trait usable both generically and behind dyn
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The Plugin trait keeps run(&self, input: &str) -> String and name(&self) -> &'static str, both taking &self with no generic method parameters and no by-value Self. That is what keeps the trait object-safe and therefore usable in Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>>. apply_one is the static-dispatch call site: fn apply_one<P: Plugin>(p: &P, input: &str) -> String. The generic bound P: Plugin means the compiler monomorphizes apply_one for each concrete type it is called with, producing a direct call. Its body formats name and run exactly as run_all does for each element, so the two paths produce identical "name => output" strings.

The dyn call site is unchanged from the chapter's listing: a Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> holding Box::new(Uppercase) and Box::new(Prefix { value: "svc-" }) compiles because the trait is object-safe, and run_all iterates that list calling through the vtable. The concrete types are erased behind one element type, Box<dyn Plugin>, while apply_one keeps the concrete type visible and resolved at compile time.

The same trait serves both call sites because it is object-safe: it declares only &self methods with no generics and no by-value Self, which is precisely the property that permits dyn. A generic bound monomorphizes to a direct call; the dyn version dispatches through a vtable; the trait definition is identical for both. apply_one(&Uppercase, "rust") yields "uppercase => RUST" and the same Uppercase inside a Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> yields the same string through run_all.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One generic call site and one dyn call site over the same unchanged, object-safe Plugin trait.
criteria: apply_one has signature fn apply_one<P: Plugin>(p: &P, input: &str) -> String and uses static dispatch via the generic bound.
The trait keeps only &self methods with no generic parameters, so Box<dyn Plugin> still compiles.
apply_one(&Uppercase, "rust") and the Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> path both produce matching "name => output" strings.
The explanation states the trait is object-safe, which is what permits both the generic and the dyn use.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a trait that cannot be boxed
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is the added generic method fn run<T: Display>(&self, input: T) -> String. It makes Plugin no longer object-safe, so Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> stops compiling. The object-safety rule it violates is that a trait method may not have its own generic type parameters (other than lifetimes). A dyn Plugin is a fat pointer to data plus a vtable, and the vtable must contain one fixed function-pointer slot per method, decided once when the trait object is created. A method generic over T would need a separate compiled instantiation for every T it is ever called with, so there is no single address to put in the slot; the compiler cannot lay out a finite vtable for an unbounded family of run<T>. At a static call site monomorphization picks the T, but at an indirect call through a vtable there is no concrete type to monomorphize against.

The fix is to remove the generic parameter and give run a concrete signature, for example fn run(&self, input: &str) -> String. That is one fixed function for every implementer, so it occupies exactly one vtable slot, and dyn dispatch works again. If implementers genuinely need to accept varied input types, the object-safe options are to accept a concrete type like &str (callers convert at the boundary) or to take &dyn Display, moving the polymorphism into a second trait object rather than a generic method.

After restoring run(&self, input: &str) -> String, the trait is object-safe again: only &self methods, no generic method parameters, no by-value Self. Box<dyn Plugin> compiles, Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> holds the heterogeneous plugins, and run_all iterates and dispatches through the vtable as before. The boxed pipeline is restored with no change to the call sites.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Removing the generic method restores one fixed vtable slot per method, so Box<dyn Plugin> compiles. The run_with helper is an optional bonus pattern, not part of the required fix.
criteria: Diagnosis names the generic method run<T> as the object-safety violation.
Explains a vtable needs one fixed slot per method, which a generic method cannot provide because each T would need its own entry.
The refactor removes the generic parameter, giving a concrete &self, input: &str method signature.
After the change, Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> and run_all compile again.

exerciseSolutions.title: Decide static versus dynamic dispatch for a processing stage API
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Use Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>. The decisive property is the combination of config-selected, heterogeneous, and runtime-assembled. Operators enable stages by configuration, so the concrete set is not known at compile time; the stages are unrelated types (normalize today; validate, redact, enrich later); and the list is built at runtime from config. A generic bound monomorphizes one homogeneous type per call and cannot hold a mixed list whose membership is decided by a config file at startup. Erasing the concrete types behind Box<dyn Stage> is exactly what lets a heterogeneous, runtime-built list share one element type and one loop.

The cost accepted with dyn is vtable indirection: each describe and run call goes through a function pointer rather than a direct, inlinable, monomorphized call, and there is no per-type specialization or cross-stage inlining. That cost is negligible here because every stage already does meaningful text work (trimming, wrapping, validating, redacting), so one indirect call per stage is lost in the noise of the per-stage processing. The pipeline is not a tight numeric inner loop where the indirection would dominate.

Keep the Stage trait object-safe from the start even though today's stages are few. Object safety is cheap to preserve now (only &self methods, no generic methods, no by-value Self) and expensive to retrofit later, because adding a generic method or a by-value Self return to a published trait is a breaking change that forecloses dyn for every existing implementer and caller. Since the entire design depends on Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>, a later edit that quietly breaks object safety would break the published API. Decide for dyn up front and hold the trait to object-safe signatures so the boxed pipeline keeps working as stages are added.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Trait objects let a config file assemble a heterogeneous stage list at runtime; object safety is preserved up front.
criteria: Selects Vec<Box<dyn Stage>> and ties it to config-driven, heterogeneous, runtime-assembled stages.
Acknowledges the vtable indirection cost and argues it is negligible relative to per-stage text work.
Commits to keeping the trait object-safe from the start to avoid a future retrofit.
Identifies that adding a generic method or by-value Self return later would foreclose dyn and break the API.

exerciseSolutions.title: Use a newtype to satisfy the orphan rule
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The orphan rule says you may implement a trait for a type only when the trait, the type, or both are local to your crate; at least one of the two must be yours. It is what keeps coherence decidable: because no two crates can both write an impl for a pair where neither side is theirs, there is never more than one impl of a trait for a type across the whole program, and trait resolution stays unambiguous.

impl Display for Vec<String> is rejected because it fails that test on both sides at once. Display lives in the standard library (std::fmt) and Vec lives in the standard library too, so neither the trait nor the type is local to your crate. Allowing it would let any crate attach its own Display to Vec<String>, and two such crates could disagree, which is exactly the ambiguity the rule forbids.

The fix is the newtype pattern: wrap the foreign type in a local tuple struct, struct Lines(Vec<String>), and implement the foreign trait for that local wrapper. Now the impl has a local type (Lines is yours) even though Display is still foreign, so the orphan rule is satisfied. Inside the impl you reach the wrapped value through self.0, since Lines is a tuple struct with a single field at index 0. The wrapper costs nothing at runtime (it is the same Vec<String> with a new name) and gives you a place to hang the impl the rule would otherwise refuse.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Wrapping the foreign Vec<String> in a local Lines newtype gives the impl a local type, so the orphan rule is satisfied.
criteria: States the orphan rule: at least one of the trait or the type must be local to the crate.
Explains the bare impl Display for Vec<String> is rejected because both Display and Vec are foreign.
Introduces a local newtype struct Lines(Vec<String>) and implements Display for Lines, which is now allowed.
Reads the wrapped value through self.0 in the Display body.

labSolution.explanation:
Two unrelated structs, Trim and Wrap, both implement one object-safe Stage trait, so Box::new(Trim) and Box::new(Wrap { tag: "b" }) can coexist in a single Vec<Box<dyn Stage>>. The trait stays object-safe because every method takes &self with no generic parameters and no by-value Self, which is the precondition for laying out the vtable that Box<dyn Stage> needs.

run_stages is a fan-out, not a chain: every stage receives the same raw input "  hi  " independently, and the output of one stage is never fed into the next. So Wrap sees the untrimmed "  hi  ", not Trim's "hi". Trim::run returns input.trim().to_string(), stripping the leading and trailing spaces from "  hi  " to produce "hi". Wrap::run returns format!("[{}]{}[/{}]", self.tag, input, self.tag), which surrounds the unmodified input with the tag, giving "[b]  hi  [/b]" (the inner spaces are preserved because Wrap receives the raw input and does not trim). Each stage is driven through the trait's default describe method, which calls self.name() and self.run(input) through the vtable and formats them as "name => output". The default method is written once on the trait yet runs for both concrete types via dynamic dispatch.

run_stages maps describe over the boxed stages and collects the lines, so the loop prints trim => hi then wrap => [b]  hi  [/b]. Finally stages.len() is 2, printing stages = 2. The output matches because the default describe method plus the two run implementations compose exactly into the expected three lines.

reviewAnswers.question: What links a concrete type to a trait in Rust, and why does that separation let one struct implement many unrelated traits?
reviewAnswers.answer: An impl block links a concrete type to a trait (impl RetryPolicy for FixedLimit); it is a separate item from both the type definition and the trait definition. Because the link lives in its own impl rather than in the type's declaration, you can add as many impls for a type as you like, each for an unrelated trait. The same struct can implement Display, Iterator, and a domain trait because none of those traits references the others; only the shared type name ties the independent impls together, which is composition over inheritance in practice.

reviewAnswers.question: How does a generic bound's dispatch differ from a trait object's dispatch, and what runtime cost does each carry?
reviewAnswers.answer: A generic bound (fn f<P: Trait>(p: &P)) is resolved at compile time by monomorphization: the compiler emits a specialized copy per concrete type with direct, inlinable calls, so the runtime cost is zero indirection at the price of code-size duplication. A trait object (&dyn Trait or Box<dyn Trait>) is resolved at runtime through a vtable: every method call goes through a function pointer, which costs one indirection per call and blocks inlining and per-type specialization. You trade compile-time specialization and speed for the ability to hold heterogeneous types behind one element type at runtime.

reviewAnswers.question: When should a trait use an associated type instead of a generic type parameter, and what symptom appears at call sites if you choose wrong?
reviewAnswers.answer: Use an associated type when each implementing type has exactly one natural output, so the implementer commits to a single answer (type Decision = bool; type Item = u8). Use a generic type parameter when the same type should implement the trait several different ways for several inputs. If you choose an associated type where you needed multiple implementations, you cannot add the second impl. If you choose a generic parameter where one output was correct, the type becomes ambiguous at call sites and callers must disambiguate with turbofish or extra type annotations to tell the compiler which instantiation they mean.

reviewAnswers.question: What does object safety require of a trait's methods, and why does each rule exist for a single indirect call through a vtable?
reviewAnswers.answer: Object safety requires that dispatchable methods take a receiver like &self or &mut self, have no generic type parameters of their own, and do not take or return Self by value. Methods that violate these rules must either be removed from the trait or bounded by where Self: Sized, which excludes them from the vtable so the remaining methods stay dispatchable; the bound is one remedy, removing the offending feature is the other. Each rule exists because a dyn Trait is a fat pointer (data plus vtable) where every dispatchable method must occupy one fixed function-pointer slot decided once. A generic method would need a different entry per T, so no single slot exists; a by-value Self appears or vanishes through a pointer whose concrete size is unknown, so it cannot be passed or returned across the indirect call. The rules guarantee one fixed, callable layout that works without knowing the concrete type.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is deciding up front whether a trait must work behind dyn important, given that adding a generic method or a by-value Self return later is a breaking change?
reviewAnswers.answer: Object safety is cheap to preserve when you design the trait but expensive to add back later. Adding a generic method or a by-value Self return to a published trait removes object safety, which breaks every existing Box<dyn Trait> and &dyn Trait use across all callers and is therefore a breaking API change. If you know the trait will be used behind dyn (for example a config-assembled plugin pipeline), commit to object-safe signatures from the start so you never have to retrofit; deciding early avoids a forced, breaking refactor of a contract you live behind for a long time.

reviewAnswers.question: What does a supertrait such as trait Audit: Identify require of every implementer, and what does it let Audit's default methods assume?
reviewAnswers.answer: Writing trait Audit: Identify makes Identify a supertrait of Audit, so every type that implements Audit must also implement Identify; the compiler refuses an Audit impl for a type that is not already an Identify. In exchange, the bodies of Audit's methods (including its default methods) may freely call the Identify methods on self, because the supertrait bound guarantees they exist. So an Audit default method like audit_line can write self.id() and trust it resolves, even though id is declared on Identify, not Audit. This is composition of requirements rather than inheritance of state: the supertrait adds a capability prerequisite to the contract without giving Audit any fields or any base-class layout, and it is the trait-level analogue of bounding a generic with Identify wherever Audit is used.
